title: Adding up the branches
objectives: Find a probability by adding every path that leads to it: the law of total probability
Weight each conditional chance by the chance of its branch, for two or more branches
See that the result is a weighted average of the conditional chances

screens.title: Adding up the branches
screens.prose: Sometimes an outcome can happen by more than one route. We will find its chance by adding up every path that leads to it.
Roll a die. On 1 or 2 you draw a counter from bag A, which holds 3 red and 1 blue. Otherwise you draw from bag B: 1 red and 3 blue.
screens.question: Tap every leaf where the counter drawn is red.

hints.text: Which bags can give a red counter?
Bag A holds 3 reds.
Both bags hold red counters, so two leaves end in red: bag A then red, and bag B then red.

feedback.correct: Red can come from either bag: two leaves.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap the leaves at the ends of the paths, one for each way to get red.

byKey.a-only: You tapped only bag A's red. Bag B holds a red counter too.
byKey.b-only: You tapped only bag B's red. Bag A holds red counters too.
byKey.a-u: That leaf is a blue counter from bag A.
byKey.b-u: That leaf is a blue counter from bag B.
byKey.a: That is a bag branch. Tap the leaves at the ends of the paths.
byKey.b: That is a bag branch. Tap the leaves at the ends of the paths.

explain.text: Red can come from either bag, so two paths end in red. Their chances are $\tfrac{1}{3} \times \tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{3}{12}$ and $\tfrac{2}{3} \times \tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{2}{12}$. A red counter means one path or the other, never both.

screens.prose: Now change how often bag A is picked. The bars show the two red paths and their total.

derive.caption: Bag A picked with chance {{fixed(pa, 2)}}: red overall {{fixed(0.75 * pa + 0.25 * (1 - pa), 3)}}

screens.question: Slide the chance of bag A from 0 to 1. Between which values does the chance of red move?

options.why: You expected the slider to reach every chance. Even with bag B certain, red has chance $\tfrac{1}{4}$.
You averaged the two bags. That is right only when each bag is equally likely, so move the slider and watch.
With bag A certain, red still has chance $\tfrac{3}{4}$, because bag A holds a blue counter.

hints.text: Drag the slider to each end and read the overall bar.
At 0, every draw comes from bag B.

feedback.correct: The chance of red always sits between the two bags' chances.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the overall bar with the slider at 0, then at 1.

explain.text: At 0 every draw is from bag B, so red has chance $\tfrac{1}{4}$. At 1 it is $\tfrac{3}{4}$. In between, the chance of red is a weighted average of the two, pulled towards the more likely bag.

screens.prose: Back to the die, where bag A has chance $\tfrac{1}{3}$. Adding the chances of every path that ends in red is the **law of total probability**.
screens.question: What is the chance the counter is red? Give a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: Find each red path's chance, then add.
The two red paths are highlighted.
$\tfrac{1}{3} \times \tfrac{3}{4} + \tfrac{2}{3} \times \tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{3}{12} + \tfrac{2}{12}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply along each red path, then add the two.

byKey.average: You averaged $\tfrac{3}{4}$ and $\tfrac{1}{4}$ as if each bag were equally likely. Bag B is picked twice as often.
byKey.a-only: That is only the path through bag A. Bag B gives red too.
byKey.b-only: That is only the path through bag B. Bag A gives red too.
byKey.added: You added $\tfrac{3}{4}$ and $\tfrac{1}{4}$ without the bag chances. Weight each by its bag.

explain.text: Bag A then red has chance $\tfrac{3}{12}$, and bag B then red has $\tfrac{2}{12}$. The paths cannot both happen, so their chances add to $\tfrac{5}{12}$. That sits between $\tfrac{1}{4}$ and $\tfrac{3}{4}$, nearer bag B's chance.

screens.prose: Now three bags of 4 counters. Bag A has 4 red, bag B has 2 red and bag C has 1 red. The die picks A on a 1, B on 2 or 3, and C on 4 to 6.

state.caption: Bag A holds no blue counter, so its blue branch is pruned

screens.question: What is the chance the counter is red? Give a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: Which leaves end in red?
Three paths end in red, one through each bag.
$\tfrac{1}{6} \times 1 + \tfrac{2}{6} \times \tfrac{2}{4} + \tfrac{3}{6} \times \tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{4}{24} + \tfrac{4}{24} + \tfrac{3}{24}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find all three red paths, multiply along each, then add.

byKey.average: You averaged 1, $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $\tfrac{1}{4}$ equally. Bag C is picked three times as often as bag A.
byKey.added: You added the bags' chances of red without weighting them, and passed 1.
byKey.c-only: That is only the path through bag C. Bags A and B give red too.

explain.text: Three paths end in red: $\tfrac{4}{24}$, $\tfrac{4}{24}$ and $\tfrac{3}{24}$. They add to $\tfrac{11}{24}$. The first stage can have any number of branches, as long as they cover every case without overlap.

screens.prose: Three new bags with the same mix. Bag A has 1 red in 4, bag B has 2 red in 8 and bag C has 3 red in 12. The same die picks the bag.
screens.question: What is the chance the counter is red? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: Chance the counter is red
widget.accept: any form equal to $\tfrac{1}{4}$, whatever the die does.

hints.text: What is the chance of red inside each bag?
Every red branch carries the same chance.
$\tfrac{1}{6} \times \tfrac{1}{4} + \tfrac{2}{6} \times \tfrac{1}{4} + \tfrac{3}{6} \times \tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{1}{4} \times 1$.

feedback.correct: Every bag gives red with chance $\tfrac{1}{4}$, so the answer is $\tfrac{1}{4}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each red branch by its bag and add.

byKey.added: You added the three red branches without the bag weights. Each one needs its weight.
byKey.third: You divided $\tfrac{1}{4}$ by the three bags. The bag weights add to 1, not to 3.

explain.text: Every red branch carries $\tfrac{1}{4}$, so $P(\text{red}) = \tfrac{1}{4} \times (\tfrac{1}{6} + \tfrac{2}{6} + \tfrac{3}{6}) = \tfrac{1}{4}$. The weights add to 1 and drop out. When red is equally likely in every bag, the bag tells you nothing about red: level 3 calls this independence.

screens.prose: Two desks book trades. Desk X books 80% of them, with an error rate of 1%. Desk Y books 20%, with an error rate of 6%. Ana says the firm's error rate is the average, 3.5%.
screens.question: What is the chance a trade picked at random has a booking error?

options.why: You averaged 0.01 and 0.06, as Ana did. Desk X books four times as many trades, so its rate counts four times as much.
You added the two error rates without weighting them by the desks' shares.
That is only desk Y's path. Desk X's errors add 0.008.

hints.text: Which leaves are errors, and what is each one's chance?
Two paths end in an error.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each desk's error rate by its share of trades, then add.

byKey.average: You took Ana's plain average. It treats the desks as equally busy, but desk X books 80% of trades.

explain.text: Desk X contributes $0.8 \times 0.01 = 0.008$ and desk Y $0.2 \times 0.06 = 0.012$. The firm's error rate is $0.02$, not Ana's $0.035$. A plain average weights each desk equally, but desk X books four times as many trades.

screens.prose: Each time, you found every path to the outcome and added them. If $A_1, \dots, A_n$ cover every case without overlap, $$P(B) = \sum_{i} P(B \mid A_i)\,P(A_i)$$ With two parts this reads $P(B) = P(B \mid A)\,P(A) + P(B \mid A^c)\,P(A^c)$.
screens.question: What must the first-stage branches do for this rule to work?

options.text: Cover every case, with no overlap

options.why: Unequal branches are fine: each term is weighted by its own $P(A_i)$, as with the desks.
If they were, every $P(B \mid A_i)$ would equal $P(B)$, and the rule would tell you nothing new.
The bags came in threes too. Any number of parts works if they cover every case once.

hints.text: What would go wrong if two branches overlapped, or a case were missing?
Overlap counts some outcomes twice, and a gap misses some. The branches must cover every case once.

feedback.correct: Each outcome must lie on exactly one path.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what adding the paths needs.

explain.text: Each outcome of $B$ must lie on exactly one path. Overlapping branches would count it twice, and a missing branch would drop it. A set of branches that covers every case once is called a partition.

screens.prose: Why is adding the paths allowed? Split the event $B$, a red counter, by the first-stage branch: $A$ is bag A, and $A^c$ is the other bag.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $B = (B \cap A) \cup (B \cap A^c)$, since every outcome is in $A$ or in $A^c$
$P(B) = P(B \cap A) + P(B \cap A^c)$, since the two pieces cannot both happen
$P(B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A) + P(A^c)\,P(B \mid A^c)$, by the multiplication rule on each piece

hints.text: Which line splits the event, before any chances appear?
Each piece of the split is one red leaf.
Split $B$, then add the two pieces' chances, then write each piece as a path product.

feedback.correct: Split, add, then multiply along each path.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start by splitting $B$, before any chances appear.

byKey.mult: The products come last. They rewrite the two chances you added.
byKey.add: You can add only after $B$ is split into pieces that do not overlap.

explain.text: The split puts each outcome of $B$ in exactly one piece, so the axiom for disjoint events lets us add. The multiplication rule then turns each piece into a path product. Those products are the red leaves you tapped on the first screen.

screens.prose: Your limit order to buy rests in the book all day. On calm days, which are 70% of days, it fills 40% of the time. On volatile days it fills 80% of the time.
screens.question: On a day picked at random, what is the chance the order fills? Give a decimal.

hints.text: Which leaves are fills?
One fill path runs through calm days, one through volatile days.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each fill rate by how often its kind of day occurs, then add.

byKey.average: You averaged 0.4 and 0.8 as if calm and volatile days were equally common. Calm days are 70% of days.
byKey.added: You added the two fill rates without weighting them by how often each kind of day occurs.
byKey.calm-only: That is only the calm-day path. Volatile days give fills too: add 0.24.
byKey.volatile-only: That is only the volatile-day path. Calm days give fills too: add 0.28.

explain.text: Calm days give $0.7 \times 0.4 = 0.28$ and volatile days $0.3 \times 0.8 = 0.24$, so the order fills with chance $0.52$. Level 2 turns the question round: given a fill, how likely is it that the day was volatile?

ideas: To find a chance, find every path that leads to it and add their chances.
Each conditional chance is weighted by its first-stage branch: $P(B) = \sum_i P(B \mid A_i)\,P(A_i)$.
The result is a weighted average of the conditional chances, so it lies between the smallest and the largest.

formula.name: Law of total probability
formula.note: With more parts, add one term per part. The parts must cover every case once.

summary.trap: Do not average or add the conditional chances on their own. Weight each one by the chance of its branch.

quiz.prose: A loan book is 50% grade A, 30% grade B and 20% grade C. Over a year their default rates are 1%, 3% and 10%.
quiz.question: What is the default rate of the whole book? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Default rate of the whole book

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each grade's default rate by its share of the book.

byKey.average: You averaged the three rates equally. Grade A is half the book, so its low rate counts most.
byKey.added: You added the three rates without weighting them by each grade's share.

explain.text: $0.5 \times 0.01 + 0.3 \times 0.03 + 0.2 \times 0.10 = 0.005 + 0.009 + 0.020 = 0.034$. Grade C is a fifth of the book but brings more than half the defaults.

quiz.prose: A stock screen flags 90% of the days before a drop and 20% of other days. A drop follows on 10% of days.
quiz.question: On a day picked at random, what is the chance the screen flags the stock? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the flag paths through drop days and through other days.

byKey.average: You averaged 0.9 and 0.2. Drop days are only 10% of days, so weight them.
byKey.drop-only: That counts only flags before drops. Most flags come on the other 90% of days.
byKey.added: You added the two rates without weighting them, and passed 1.

explain.text: Drop days give $0.1 \times 0.9 = 0.09$ and other days $0.9 \times 0.2 = 0.18$. So the screen flags on $0.27$ of days. Two thirds of the flags come on days with no drop.

quiz.prose: A signal fires on 30% of days in a bull market, 30% in a flat market and 30% in a bear market. Bull, flat and bear markets make up 50%, 30% and 20% of days.
quiz.question: On a day picked at random, what is the chance the signal fires?

options.why: You added the three 30% rates without the market weights.
You divided 0.3 by the three markets. The market weights add to 1, not 3.
That is only the bull-market path. The other markets add 0.09 and 0.06.

feedback.correct: Every market gives 0.3, so the weights drop out.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each market's rate, then add.

explain.text: $0.5 \times 0.3 + 0.3 \times 0.3 + 0.2 \times 0.3 = 0.3 \times 1 = 0.3$. When the rate is the same in every branch, the weights add to 1 and drop out.

quiz.prose: Two cards are dealt from a standard deck without replacement. Nobody sees the first card.
quiz.question: What is the chance the second card is a heart?

options.why: That assumes the first card was a heart. Nobody saw it, so both branches count.
That assumes the first card was not a heart. Nobody saw it, so both branches count.
That is only heart, then heart. Add the path not a heart, then heart.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two paths that end in a heart.

explain.text: Heart, then heart gives $\tfrac{13}{52} \times \tfrac{12}{51} = \tfrac{156}{2652}$. Not a heart, then heart gives $\tfrac{39}{52} \times \tfrac{13}{51} = \tfrac{507}{2652}$. They add to $\tfrac{663}{2652} = \tfrac{1}{4}$, the same as the first card.
